title: The Footbridge
objective: After this level you can explain why many people who would pull the switch refuse to push a man off a footbridge, and how the doctrine of double effect tries to explain the difference.
summary: Thomson’s footbridge keeps five for one, yet many who would switch refuse to push; double effect explains it by intended means versus foreseen side effect, and critics raise the problem of closeness.

cards.headline: Same five, same one. Why does pushing feel so different from pulling?
cards.body: Many people who would pull a lever to save five refuse to push one person to do it. The count hasn’t changed. Something else has.

cards.headline: Thomson’s footbridge
cards.body: Judith Jarvis Thomson set out the case in 1985, building on Foot’s examples from 1967. A trolley is heading for five people who can’t escape. You’re on a footbridge above the track, next to a heavy stranger. The only way to stop the trolley is to push him off, onto the track. The trade is exactly the switch case’s: one for five.

cards.headline: Many say no
cards.body: Many people believe pushing him would be wrong, yet switching the trolley onto a track with one person would be permissible. If only the number of lives mattered, the two cases would get the same answer. So philosophers set out to name the difference that seems to be doing the work.

cards.headline: Means or side effect?
cards.body: One answer is the doctrine of double effect, credited to Thomas Aquinas. It separates harm you cause as a means to a good end from harm you cause only as a foreseen side effect. At the switch, the one person’s death is a foreseen side effect of diverting the trolley. On the bridge, his body stopping the trolley is the plan itself. On this view, that makes pushing wrong.

cards.headline: Critics push back
cards.body: Critics raise the problem of closeness. Some harms sit so close to the means that it’s hard to call them merely foreseen, and no clear way of drawing that line has emerged. Others split differently: some take the switch and push intuitions as proof of double effect, Thomson in 2008 denied that switching is allowed at all, and McIntyre denied that double effect explains the switch case.

cards.headline: The Footbridge: the big picture
learned: Many who would switch refuse to push
Double effect: means versus side effect

questions.prompt: What does the doctrine of double effect distinguish?

options.label: Harms done to strangers from harms done to your own friends
options.rationale: It is about means and side effects, not relationships.

options.label: Harm caused as a means from harm only foreseen as a side effect
Harms that happen quickly from harms that build up slowly
Harms that the law forbids from harms that the law allows
options.rationale: It is a moral principle, not a legal one.

questions.explanation: Double effect separates grave harm caused as a means to a good end from harm caused only as a foreseen side effect.

questions.prompt: Many would switch the trolley but refuse to push. Which explanation is the one double effect gives, rather than a count of lives?

options.label: Pushing the man would save fewer people than switching would
options.rationale: Both cases trade one for five.

options.label: The man on the bridge chose to stand there, so he accepted the risk
options.rationale: His choice plays no part in double effect.

options.label: Pushing makes the man’s death the means of saving the five
The switch is further from the five people than the bridge is
options.rationale: Distance is not the principle’s concern.

questions.explanation: On double effect, the switch case’s death is a foreseen side effect, but pushing makes the man’s death the means of saving the five.

questions.prompt: The footbridge keeps the switch case’s one-for-five trade and changes only how the one is harmed. Which Level 3 design idea does that follow?

options.label: Add as many vivid details as you can
Test the case on a real bridge before judging
Let each reader choose the numbers
options.rationale: The numbers are fixed on purpose.

options.label: Change one thing and leave everything else alone

questions.explanation: Like Gyges’s ring, the footbridge removes or changes one thing and holds the rest still, so any change in verdict points at that one difference.
